summary:
Nuevo León's penal code contains no transfeminicide offence, and the state's 2019 hate-crime provision covers sexual orientation but not gender identity. A trans visitor assaulted in Monterrey therefore faces a legal framework with no category naming the bias used against them.

Killings in mid-2024 were concentrated and public. Agencia Presentes reported on 31 July 2024 that three trans women were killed in Nuevo León in under a week: Arantza Castillo, 23, shot while doing sex work, and a victim found in a motel on 27 June who was still unidentified. The state justice ministry issued no case information on either killing.

Counts for the year differ but agree on scale. Verificado recorded 7 attacks on LGBT people, 3 forced disappearances and 4 transfeminicides in Nuevo León during 2024. Letra S's yearbook, the country's longest-running civil-society hate-crime observatory, running since 1998, ranked Nuevo León second among Mexican states with 5 LGBT+ homicides in 2024, behind Mexico City's 17, of which 11 were trans women. The Asamblea Nacional Trans No Binarie counted at least 36 trans women transfemicided nationally in 2024, at least four of them in Nuevo León.

Activists reported six trans women killed within a short period and accused municipal, state and national authorities of rights omissions.

The legislative response has been refusal. Colectivo Casa Trans held a plantón outside the Nuevo León congress for more than 50 days, pressing legislators to typify transfeminicidio in the state penal code; the collective's bill was ignored for a year and lapsed, forcing a fresh filing (ABC Noticias, 12 January 2026).

Nuevo León does maintain an anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2 to 5 years' imprisonment. The national observatory's assessment of such statutes is that transfeminicide advances in law but not in sentences.
tangentialFactors:
Extending legal gender recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of Mexican equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, while calling on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them and warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Barriers are documented concretely. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Violence against trans people intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
A labour diagnostic survey of Nuevo León found 42.2% of the state's trans population unemployed and 35.1% discriminated against at work, conditions that shape where residents can live and how visible they can be.

Residents seeking to correct name and gender markers on identity documents do so under the patchwork of state-level administrative procedures described by Human Rights Watch, with implementation varying sharply between states and no source in this inventory confirming the procedure available in Nuevo León.

The anti-conversion-practices law carrying 2 to 5 years' imprisonment binds practitioners within the state, and the plantón by Colectivo Casa Trans outside the state congress is a resident-led campaign directed at the state legislature rather than at visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Nuevo León operates an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, and what documents a trans resident can obtain there, is unresolved in this inventory; the Human Rights Watch reporting establishes only that procedures differ widely between Mexican states.

Case outcomes for the July 2024 killings are unresolved. The state justice ministry issued no case information, and no source here records arrests, charges or convictions in any of the four transfeminicides attributed to the state for 2024.

Whether the 2019 hate-crime provision has ever been applied to a gender-identity motive is not sourced, nor is the enforcement record of the anti-conversion-practices law.

Counts of killings are known to understate the total: Letra S notes that Mexico has no official registry of bias-motivated violence and that media accounts frequently lack victim names and gender data, so the figures for Nuevo León should be read as a floor rather than a settled total.
